opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that once you actually build the hardware yourself, you stop treating the gripper as a solved, boring component and start seeing it as the place where a lot of the intelligence either gets enabled or gets thrown away.

When you only work in simulation or only on the learning side, a parallel-jaw gripper looks like a perfectly reasonable abstraction. You open, you close, you get a binary grasp. And honestly, for a lot of pick-and-place benchmarks, it works surprisingly well. But when you're in the lab building fingers, wiring sensors, breaking things, you realize how much of manipulation is about what happens *after* first contact: sliding an object to reorient it, feeling whether it's slipping, using the fingertip to push something into a corner before you lift it. A simple two-finger gripper basically can't do most of that. It doesn't have the degrees of freedom, and usually it doesn't have the sensing either.

The other thing hardware teaches you is humility about the gap between what the policy "wants" and what the mechanism can physically deliver. You'll have a model that's learned a nice behavior from human demonstrations, but the human was using a hand with dozens of contact points and rich tactile feedback, and you're asking a rigid jaw to reproduce it. So a lot of failures that people blame on the learning algorithm are actually embodiment failures. You only really internalize that when you've debugged it at the bench.

That said, I don't think the lesson is simply "dexterous hands good, grippers bad." Building hardware also makes you painfully aware of the costs: complexity, reliability, price, how quickly a tendon-driven finger wears out. Simple grippers are simple for a reason. They're robust, cheap, and easy to model. So my judgment now is more about matching the hand to the task and the data. For the long tail of household manipulation, things like folding, tool use, handling deformable or tiny objects, I'm convinced simple grippers hit a ceiling pretty fast. But the right answer is probably something in between: designs that add just enough compliance, sensing, and a few extra degrees of freedom to unlock in-hand manipulation, while staying practical enough to actually deploy and collect lots of data with.

So hands-on R&D didn't just make me more critical of simple grippers. It made me think of hardware and learning as one co-design problem rather than two separate fields.

r001.rationale: The response recommends matching the hand to the task and adding capabilities, but does not identify swapping in a task-specific gripper as the solution.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes embodiment failures from learning-algorithm failures, but does not state that hands-on R&D separates fundamental robotics problems from easy-to-solve ones.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, before I actually sat down and built grippers myself, I had the same intuition most people in the field have, which is that the two-finger parallel gripper is a kind of placeholder. Something you use until the real thing, the dexterous hand, arrives. And then you get your hands dirty, literally, and that view gets complicated very quickly.

The first thing you learn is that most of what you thought were limitations of the gripper were actually limitations of perception and control. You watch a simple gripper fail to pick up a cup, and your instinct says, "it needs more fingers." But then you look at the logs and you realize the grasp point was off by a centimeter, or the approach trajectory squeezed the handle in a way no human would. The hardware was fine. The brain was wrong. So hands-on work makes you much more careful about attributing failure. You stop blaming the hand reflexively.

The second thing is that you develop real respect for how much a two-finger gripper can do if you treat the environment as part of the hand. Humans do this constantly. We push a coin to the edge of a table before we pick it up. We lean a book against another book. When I started building, I was surprised how many tasks that looked like they required dexterity actually required cleverness about contact with surfaces. A rigid gripper with good compliance in the wrist and good tactile sensing in the fingertips covers a far larger share of real tasks than the benchmark videos suggest.

But, and this is the part that I think only hardware experience teaches you, there are failure modes that are genuinely physical and no amount of software fixes them. Thin, flat objects on a flat surface. Deformable things, like a plastic bag, where the gripper closes and the object just reshapes around it. In-hand reorientation, where you need to rotate something without putting it down. When you've spent weeks tuning finger pads and watching the same slip happen a hundred times, you stop being romantic about it. You know exactly where the wall is, because you've hit it.

So I'd say the net effect is that it makes your judgment less ideological in both directions. The people who say simple grippers are enough are usually looking at a narrow distribution of tasks. The people who say we must have humanoid hands are usually underestimating how much of the problem is upstream of the fingers. Having built the thing, I'd put it this way: the gripper is almost never the first bottleneck, but it is a real bottleneck, and you only find out which one you're facing by building and failing repeatedly rather than reasoning from the armchair.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the capabilities and limits of a two-finger gripper, but does not identify swapping in a task-specific gripper as a solution.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes failures caused by perception and control—such as a misplaced grasp point—from genuinely physical limits that software cannot fix.

astra-6.text:
I think hands-on hardware R&D makes you much more specific about what a gripper’s limitation actually is. When a grasp fails, is it because you don’t have enough degrees of freedom? Or is the object slightly out of position, the friction different than you expected, or the force control too crude? Those can look like the same failure, but they call for very different solutions.

A simple gripper can do a surprising amount if you choose the contact surfaces well, add some compliance, and approach the object intelligently. But once you need to reorient something within the hand, handle very different shapes, or recover from a slip, its mechanical limits become much clearer.

So I’d judge it by how reliably it performs across the variation the task actually involves. Getting one successful grasp is useful; understanding why it fails on the next twenty attempts is what tells you whether you need a better controller, a better gripper, or a different approach.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving or replacing the gripper generally, but does not identify swapping in a task-specific gripper.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes possible causes of grasp failure and the solutions they call for, but does not state that hands-on R&D separates fundamental robotics problems from problems that are easy to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
Once you build and test hardware yourself, you become much more careful about what you mean by “simple.” A two-finger gripper can look very limited, but with the right contact surfaces, a little compliance, and a well-designed task, it can do a surprising amount. And a more complicated hand can still fail because the object slips or the sensing isn’t good enough.

So hands-on R&D makes me ask: is this really a limitation of the gripper, or of how we’re approaching the task? Can we change the grasp, use the table for support, or adjust the motion? The limitation becomes much clearer when you need reliable performance across different objects and repeated trials. Picking something up once is very different from making it work consistently.

r001.rationale: The response suggests changing contact surfaces, compliance, grasp, support, or motion, but it does not identify swapping in a task-specific gripper.
